sourceBindings.text: A soil report is only as useful as the sample and the record behind it. Before touching a sample or test kit, identify the hazards, choose the right tools and protect the sample's identity from field to laboratory.

Under trainer supervision, locate the site's emergency and waste facilities, read the relevant label and SDS, choose compatible eye, body and hand protection, and demonstrate the correct weighing, volume, mixing and sieving tools.

Personally prepare an assigned soil sample using the receiving laboratory's method: record its identity, dry it when required and document the real wait, gently break aggregates without grinding stones, pass the required fraction through a 2 mm sieve when this protocol calls for it, and protect against cross-contamination.

For the final-product task, submit the learner's own prepared, sealed sample weighing 450–550 g with the full field/date/depth/collector label, and explain why air-drying is not suitable for every analysis.

sourceBindings.text: A procedure calls for 20 mL of distilled water. A learner wants to read it from a beaker's rough scale.
The beaker is suitable for holding and mixing, but the graduated cylinder is the specified measured-volume tool.
Read the cylinder correctly in mL, then transfer to the beaker without contaminating either sample.
The later pH step will use the method's ratio; do not change it by guessing from a beaker.
Match tool precision to the procedure.

sourceBindings.text: A moist soil sample arrives without a requested analysis on its submission form.
Maintain its identity and ask the receiving laboratory or trainer what analysis and preservation are required.
Do not air-dry simply because routine fertility samples often are; some targets can change or be lost.
If routine air-drying is confirmed, begin a logged, labelled thin-layer drying stage and finish by the method's condition.
The method determines preparation, not the moisture alone.

sourceBindings.text: The final preparation task asks for an approximately 500 g sample made from moist field soil with roots, twigs and stones.
Document the learner's own method-approved drying and gentle crushing/sieving, maintaining the same field ID.
Weigh 450–550 g of the prepared fine soil into a suitable bag for this assessment, seal it and confirm no debris or spill.
Write date, Field ID, sampling depth and collector's name legibly and match the field record. The product proves a correct bag only when the observed process is also recorded.
The 450–550 g tolerance is this card's criterion, not a universal lab shipping rule.

sourceBindings.text: Safety Data Sheet (SDS)
Chemical-specific hazard, first-aid, handling and protection information; formerly called MSDS.
PPE
Personal protective equipment selected for the task and material, not a universal glove or goggle type.
aggregate
A clump of natural soil particles that can be gently separated during this preparation.
2 mm sieve
Screen with 2 mm openings used for the fine-earth fraction in this teaching protocol.
fine-earth fraction
Soil material passing the specified sieve, while larger stones and debris are separated.
sample traceability
The continuous link between the field record, trays, subsamples, test results and final bag.
